posts.title: The behavior of red foxes
posts.body: Red foxes are solitary hunters that are most active at dawn and dusk. They pounce on mice hidden under snow, cache surplus food and use a wide range of vocalisations. This guide explains how red foxes hunt, communicate and raise their kits.

posts.title: What does Vulpes vulpes eat?
posts.body: Vulpes vulpes is an opportunistic omnivore. Its diet includes small rodents, rabbits, birds, insects, berries and fruit. Urban populations also scavenge food waste. We look at how its diet changes across seasons.

posts.title: Fox kits in spring: a wild fox family
posts.body: Every spring a vixen gives birth to a litter of kits in an underground den. By five weeks old the young foxes emerge to play near the entrance while both parents bring food. Here is what to expect if a wild fox family moves in nearby.

posts.title: How gray wolf packs hunt together
posts.body: Gray wolves hunt cooperatively in packs led by a breeding pair. Canis lupus can bring down prey many times larger than a single wolf, such as elk and moose, by coordinating chases and testing herds for weak animals.

posts.title: Why do wolves howl?
posts.body: Wolves howl to assemble the pack, mark territory and communicate over long distances. A single howl can carry for kilometres in a forest. Researchers can even identify individual timber wolves from their howls.

posts.title: Puppy training basics for new dog owners
posts.body: Training a puppy starts on day one. Use short sessions, reward good behaviour with treats and teach sit, stay and recall. Consistency and patience turn an energetic young dog into a well-mannered companion.

posts.title: Why daily walks keep your dog healthy
posts.body: Regular walks give dogs exercise, mental stimulation and social contact. Most adult dogs need at least 30 to 60 minutes a day. We cover leash training, walking in hot weather and signs your dog needs more activity.

posts.title: How brown bears survive hibernation
posts.body: Brown bears spend up to seven months in their dens without eating or drinking. Ursus arctos lowers its heart rate and recycles waste proteins, then emerges in spring thinner but healthy. Here is the science of bear hibernation.

posts.title: Grizzly bears and the salmon run
posts.body: Each summer grizzly bears gather at rivers to catch salmon swimming upstream. A large grizzly can eat dozens of fish a day to build fat reserves before winter, standing in rapids and waterfalls to snatch leaping salmon.

posts.title: The autumn rut: when deer stags compete
posts.body: During the autumn rut, stags roar, thrash vegetation and lock antlers to compete for does. Red deer and white-tailed deer both show dramatic behaviour in this season, which is the best time for wildlife photographers.

posts.title: Found a fawn alone? Leave it be
posts.body: A young fawn lying quietly in tall grass is usually not abandoned. The doe leaves her fawn hidden while she feeds nearby and returns several times a day. Here is when to leave a fawn alone and when to call wildlife rescue.

posts.title: How to make a sourdough starter at home
posts.body: A sourdough starter needs only flour and water. Feed it daily, keep it warm, and in about a week it will bubble and rise predictably. We explain hydration, discard and how to tell when your starter is ready to bake bread.

posts.title: Why coral reefs are bleaching
posts.body: Coral bleaching happens when warm water stresses corals and they expel the algae living in their tissues. Without the algae the coral turns white and can starve. Rising ocean temperatures have caused mass bleaching events worldwide.

posts.title: How the arctic hare stays hidden
posts.body: The arctic hare turns white in winter to blend into snow and ice, and huddles in groups to stay warm. Its large hind feet act like snowshoes. This article explains the camouflage and survival strategies of the arctic hare.
